title: Design a data structure that supports adding integers from a stream and returning the median of all values added so far, in logarithmic add time and constant median time.
shortTitle: Find Median from Data Stream — two heaps (max-heap lower + min-heap upper)

s1_definition.profdef: Two balanced heaps split the stream in half: a max-heap holds the lower half so its top is the largest of the small values, and a min-heap holds the upper half so its top is the smallest of the large values. The heaps are kept balanced in size, so the median is either the max-heap top (odd count) or the average of both tops (even count).
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine tracking the median transaction amount as amounts stream in all day. You keep two piles: a low pile ordered so the biggest low value sits on top, and a high pile ordered so the smallest high value sits on top. You keep the piles nearly equal in height, so the median is right at the boundary — either the top of the bigger pile or the average of the two tops.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, balanced in size; the median is the larger heap's top or the average of both tops.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Two balanced heaps split the stream in half: a max-heap holds the lower half so its top is the largest of the small values, and a min-heap holds the upper half so its top is the smallest of the large values. The heaps are kept balanced in size, so the median is either the max-heap top (odd count) or the average of both tops (even count).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine tracking the median transaction amount as amounts stream in all day. You keep two piles: a low pile ordered so the biggest low value sits on top, and a high pile ordered so the smallest high value sits on top. You keep the piles nearly equal in height, so the median is right at the boundary — either the top of the bigger pile or the average of the two tops.

**One line to remember:** Keep a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, balanced in size; the median is the larger heap's top or the average of both tops.

sections.s2_technical:
Maintain a max-heap called low and a min-heap called high. On each add, push to low first, then move low's top to high to ensure every element in low is no larger than every element in high. For example: `low.offer(x); high.offer(low.poll());`.

Rebalance so the heaps differ in size by at most one, keeping low at least as large as high. If high grows larger than low, move high's top back to low. For example: `if (high.size() > low.size()) low.offer(high.poll());`. This ordering and balancing are the invariants that place the median at the boundary.

To read the median, if the total count is odd then low holds one extra element and its top is the median; if even, the median is the average of low's top and high's top. For example: `return low.size() > high.size() ? low.peek() : (low.peek() + high.peek()) / 2.0;`.

Each add does a constant number of heap operations, each log n, so add is log n and median read is constant. A senior nuance is the push-then-shift pattern that guarantees correct partitioning without comparing against both tops manually, and choosing which heap holds the extra element consistently so the odd-count median is unambiguous. Integer overflow in the average should be handled with care for large values.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a monitoring service reports the running median transaction amount as amounts stream in, to detect drift from normal behavior. The system must add amounts and query the median efficiently at any time. This is exactly how Find Median from Data Stream works — two heaps maintain the median incrementally.

Problem 2 — Sorting the whole history on every query would be far too slow for a live stream. This is exactly why two balanced heaps are used, giving logarithmic add and constant median.

The mini-project builds a `RunningMedian` service over the two heaps, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo that streams amounts and prints the median after each.

sections.s5_journey:
The input stream is 5000, 3000, 8000, 1000, 10000.

Step 1: Add 5000. It goes into low then shifts to high, then rebalances back into low. Low holds 5000, high empty. Count one is odd, median is 5000.

Step 2: Add 3000. Pushed to low then its top 5000 shifts to high, leaving low with 3000 and high with 5000. Count two is even, median is the average of 3000 and 5000, which is 4000.

Step 3: Add 8000. Pushed to low, low's top shifts to high, then rebalance returns the smaller to low. Low holds 5000, high holds 8000, and low has the extra, so median is 5000.

Step 4: Add 1000. After the push-shift-rebalance, low holds 1000 and 3000 wait — low holds the lower two and high the upper two, count four is even, median is the average of the two boundary tops, which is 4000.

Step 5: Add 10000. Count five is odd, the heaps settle with low holding the extra element and its top being 5000, so the median is 5000.

Step 6: Throughout, each add did only a few heap operations and the median was read from the tops in constant time.

sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  add(x): low.offer(x); high.offer(low.poll());
          if high.size > low.size: low.offer(high.poll())

   low (max-heap, lower half)   |   high (min-heap, upper half)
         top = largest low      |   top = smallest high
                      ↘ median ↙
   odd  → low.top
   even → (low.top + high.top)/2

  stream 5000,3000,8000,1000,10000 → medians 5000,4000,5000,4000,5000
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Find Median from Data Stream asks for the running median with fast adds and instant median reads, which rules out re-sorting the history each query. My solution keeps two heaps that split the data at the median: a max-heap for the lower half, so its top is the largest small value, and a min-heap for the upper half, so its top is the smallest large value.

On each add I push the new value into the low heap, then move low's top into the high heap, which guarantees every element in low is no larger than every element in high. Then I rebalance so the two heaps differ in size by at most one, keeping low at least as large, by moving high's top back if high ever grows bigger. These invariants place the median exactly at the boundary: with an odd count low holds the extra element and its top is the median, and with an even count the median is the average of the two tops.

The detail interviewers listen for is the push-then-shift pattern, which partitions correctly without manually comparing against both tops, plus consistently choosing which heap carries the extra element so the odd-count median is unambiguous, and being careful with overflow when averaging large values. Each add is a constant number of log n heap operations and the median read is constant.

In my project at National Bank of India, a monitoring service reported the running median transaction amount as amounts streamed in all day, to catch drift from normal behavior. The two-heap structure let every amount be absorbed in logarithmic time and the median be read instantly on each tick, so the monitor stayed real-time instead of re-sorting the growing history on every query.
